title: Fixing A Problem Is Not the Same as Fixing THE Problem
author: Bootleg Manager
summary: Using an extended doctor's-office analogy (a sore toe treated by amputation rather than diagnosis), this Leadership essay catalogs the reasons managers and executives default to fast, plausible-looking fixes instead of investigating root causes. The author walks through several recurring failure modes: time pressure that makes any action feel better than a proper diagnosis, pattern-matching from past experience that misapplies a familiar fix to a novel problem, infatuation with a new tool that becomes a hammer for every nail, and simple burnout that makes people stop caring about getting it right. Concrete workplace parallels are drawn throughout, from adding status meetings to fix missed deadlines to mandating training to fix process failures to hiring more salespeople to fix a revenue shortfall, each an example of treating a symptom instead of the underlying system. The essay's central distinction, between 'problem solving' and 'problem seeing,' argues that most organizational dysfunction stems from skipping investigation in favor of an immediately available, socially acceptable-looking action. The piece closes by previewing further writing on this theme, signaling it is part of an ongoing series on root-cause thinking.
points: Distinguishes 'problem solving' from 'problem seeing,' arguing organizations habitually reach for fast, visible fixes without diagnosing the actual root cause.
Catalogs specific failure modes: time pressure, pattern-matching from past experience, infatuation with a new tool, and simple burnout, each illustrated with a workplace parallel.

Uses concrete business examples (more status meetings for missed deadlines, more training for process failures, more salespeople for a revenue shortfall) as recognizable instances of symptom-only fixes.
Argues that surface fixes are often chosen specifically because they let decision-makers avoid the expensive, uncomfortable work of investigating what's actually broken.
quotes: Knee-jerk reactions tend to have consequences. The problem in front of you is not necessarily THE problem.
In my experience, if someone comes up with an immediate solution to a problem, it pays to be wary. Because what you're seeing may not be so easily explained, let alone solved.
When time is of the essence, doing something is better than doing nothing. In their rush, people decide that a proper diagnosis will take too long.
We rely on what's familiar to color our judgment. If it worked before, it'll work again.

Lasers aren't always the solution. Neither are databases. Or whatever particular hammer you might have at the moment. It pays to figure out if what's in front of you is actually a nail before you take a swing at it.
Fixing the surface problem allows you to avoid whatever expensive, complicated, distasteful things might be beneath it.
